```{r}
library(tidyverse)
#import data
ielts <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2026/2026-08-18/demo_by_first_language.csv"
)
#data cleaning
glimpse(ielts)
ielts_clean <- ielts |>
  filter(
    !is.na(language),
    !is.na(band),
    !is.na(percent),
    !is.na(type)
  )
glimpse(ielts_clean)
```
```{r}
head(ielts)
str(ielts)
```
**1. RQ1: What is the overall distribution of IELTS scores?** 【Which I might put question in front tobe the general question.】
```{r}
#| label: fig-ielts-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of IELTS band scores based on the average percentage at each band."
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart showing the average percentage for each IELTS band. The distribution peaks at bands 6.0 and 6.5, both around about 17% to 18%, while lower and higher bands have smaller percentages."
ielts_clean |>
  group_by(band) |>
  summarise(avg_percent = mean(percent)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = band, y = avg_percent)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of IELTS Scores",
    x = "IELTS Band",
    y = "Average Percentage"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
**Research Question 1 Findings**
The distribution of IELTS scores is slightly skewed to the left, with the highest average percentages occurring at bands 6.0 and 6.5 (around 18%). Most scores are concentrated between 5.5 and 7.5, while extremely low and high scores are relatively uncommon.The results suggest that intermediate IELTS band levels are more common than extreme scores across the groups represented in the dataset.



**2. RQ2: How do IELTS score distributions differ across first-language groups (Chinese, Japanese, Korean,French, Arab)?**
```{r}
#| label: fig-ielts-language
#| fig-cap: "Comparison of IELTS score distributions across five first-language groups."
#| fig-alt: "Five bar charts comparing the average percentage of IELTS scores across different band levels for Chinese, Japanese, Korean, French, and Arabic speakers."

ielts_clean |>
  filter(language %in% c("Chinese", "Japanese", "Korean",
                         "French", "Arabic")) |>
  group_by(language, band) |>
  summarise(avg_percent = mean(percent) * 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = band, y = avg_percent)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", fill = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~language) +
  labs(
    title = "IELTS Score Distribution by First Language",
    x = "IELTS Band",
    y = "Average Percentage (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
```{r}
ielts_clean |>
  filter(language %in% c("Chinese", "Japanese", "Korean",
                         "French", "Arabic")) |>
  mutate(
    score_category = case_when(
      band %in% c("<4", "4", "4.5", "5") ~ "Low",
      band %in% c("5.5", "6", "6.5") ~ "Medium",
      band %in% c("7", "7.5", "8", "8.5", "9") ~ "High"
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(language, type, year, score_category) |>
  summarise(category_percent = sum(percent), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(language, score_category) |>
  summarise(avg_percent = mean(category_percent), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = language, y = avg_percent,
             fill = score_category)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "fill") +
  labs(
    title = "IELTS Score Categories by First Language",
    x = "First Language",
    y = "Proportion",
    fill = "Score Category"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Research question2 findings**
IELTS score distributions vary across the five first-language groups. Chinese and Korean speakers show similar distributions, the highest average percentages at band 6.0 (approximately 21% and 22%, respectively). Japanese and Arabic speakers have distributions concentrated at relatively lower bands, especially between 5.0 and 6.0. French speakers have a distribution shifted toward higher scores, the relatively large percentages between bands 6.0 and 7.5.

**3. RQ3: Which first-language groups have the highest proportions of IELTS scores of 7.0 or above, and how does this differ by test type?**

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of IELTS high-score percentages across language groups, test types, and reporting periods."
#| fig-alt: "Histogram showing the distribution of percentages of IELTS scores of 7.0 or above across language groups, test types, and reporting periods."

ielts_clean |>
  filter(band %in% c("7", "7.5", "8", "8.5", "9")) |>
  group_by(language, type, year) |>
  summarise(high_percent = sum(percent) * 100,
            .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = high_percent)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue",
                 color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of IELTS High-Score Percentages",
    x = "Percentage of Scores 7.0+ (%)",
    y = "Number of observations(Number of Language–Test–Year Groups)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
**research question 3 finding:**


The histogram shows that most IELTS high-score percentages are concentrated between 15% and 50%, with the highest frequency occurring at 35%. The distribution is slightly right-skewed, small number of observations have high-score percentages over 55% to 60%, with a few reaching nearly 90%. The results suggest that the proportion of IELTS scores of 7.0 or above varies considerably across language groups, test types, and reporting periods.
